Part I of On Living closes: I mean, you must take living so seriously / that even at seventy, for example, you’ll plant olive trees— / and not for your children, either, / but because although you fear death you don’t believe it, / because living, I mean, weighs heavier. That matches the card to the letter, curly apostrophes and the em dash after olive trees included, with the same lineation and lower-case line heads. The page credit reads From Poems of Nazim Hikmet, translated by Randy Blasing and Mutlu Konuk, published by Persea Books, copyright 1994, so the named translation and year are the ones whose wording this is. The locator is right: these are the last five lines of Part I (not of the whole poem), and the source says Part I. shipped.js: not shipped, no near opening, Hikmet at 0 of 3, not banned. Not on the misattribution list. In scope: a poem written 1947 to 1948, not a lyric or speech. Publishable: death is named only to be outweighed by living, which is the month's hope. Source line 121 characters, leads with the name, no dash; the em dash is inside the quotation as the translators' own punctuation, which the rules allow. Two soft points, neither a refutation: the byline spells Nâzim while the book title spells Nazim and the Turkish is Nâzım, so the editor may want one spelling (Nazim matches the translation's credit); and fame rests on the olive-trees passage being the poem's most quoted lines rather than on a closing line of the whole work.
